blocks.heading: A PROJECT THAT DEMANDED MORE THAN DESIGN
What This Project Taught Me About Opportunity & Commitment

As a branding designer and visual artist, it is rare to find a project that *demands equal attention from both disciplines.* When that opportunity comes through two clients you deeply respect—in this case Royal Enfield and UNESCO—it feels almost unreal.

The Great Himalayan Exploration was a programme focused on documenting and celebrating the rich Intangible Cultural Heritage (ICH) of the Himalayan region while promoting sustainable tourism and cultural preservation.

The *opportunity* itself was *extraordinary.*

The commitment it demanded was even greater.

*Before formally taking on the project, the first question was not about creativity—it was about time. There was an immense amount to be accomplished within an incredibly compressed timeline.* <ref n="01"/>

annotations.text: 20 days to launch. Every decision, from strategy to execution, had to happen in parallel.

blocks.heading: DESIGNING FOR SOMETHING YOU CAN'T SELL

On one side was the responsibility of creating a brand identity and communication system for something that wasn't a product, a service, or a company. It was an idea. An emotion. A celebration of traditions, crafts, music, stories, food, and ways of life that have been passed down through generations across the Himalayan landscape.

blocks.leftColumn: *Designing for emotion requires a different kind of responsibility.*
blocks.rightColumn: Beyond research and strategy, it demands empathy. It requires time to pause, reflect, and connect with the people whose stories are being represented. More than satisfying UNESCO or Royal Enfield, it needed to feel authentic to the communities whose heritage was being celebrated.

blocks.heading:
At the same time, an art installation was to be developed for the launch event.

The challenge was immense. Within a matter of days, we had to conceptualise, create, and execute an installation inspired by the indigenous art, craft, and cultural narratives of the Himalayan region.

Nine helmets and six motorcycle tanks became our canvas.
THE HIMALAYAS AS A STARTING POINT

Each piece was inspired by a different aspect of the region—its visual traditions, its landscapes, its people, and its stories. Some artworks drew directly from indigenous motifs, while others attempted to capture the spirit of the Himalayas from a broader, more contemplative perspective.

Every surface became a journey.

If not a journey through geography, then a journey through time.

For days, the project consumed every waking hour. Sketching, painting, refining, and problem-solving became a continuous cycle. *What finally emerged across my worktable was not merely a collection of painted objects, but a series of narratives brought to life through form and colour.*

I was fortunate to have unwavering support from *Ayush Singh* from the PMDIndia *Team,* whose dedication and involvement helped bring the installation to completion.<ref n="02"/>

The installation itself was titled ‘*The Winds of Change.’*

annotations.text: 11 days in. A major milestone was behind us, but the finish line still felt distant.

blocks.heading: Beyond the artwork, there were practical challenges to solve. Custom structures had to be designed to support the pieces, spatial compositions had to be planned, and every element had to come together seamlessly before the event opened its doors.

*Simultaneously, the branding work reached completion.*<ref n="03"/> With three days remaining, the branding work finally crossed the finish line. The identity system, visual language, and communication framework were developed within an incredibly demanding timeline. The response from both teams was encouraging, particularly toward the identity mark, which became the central element tying the entire initiative together.

What made the experience memorable was not that everything came together perfectly.

It was that everything came together at all.

Within roughly two weeks, an idea had become a brand, an installation, a launch event, and a shared experience.

annotations.text: Three days remained. For the first time, the project felt ready.

blocks.heading:
The inauguration at Bikaner House, New Delhi brought together representatives from UNESCO, Royal Enfield, government bodies, artists, artisans, and cultural practitioners from across the Himalayan region. People representing music, weaving, food, craft, storytelling, and tradition stood together within the very space we had spent days imagining.

*The satisfaction wasn't in hearing that people liked the work.* It was looking around the room and seeing the very people whose stories had inspired the project standing beside it. Artisans, musicians, cultural practitioners, and representatives from across the Himalayan region had all become part of the same moment.

That's when the project felt *complete.*
THE LESSON STAYED LONGER THAN THE EVENT

And perhaps that is what this project taught me.

Opportunities often arrive disguised as impossible timelines, overwhelming responsibilities, and challenges that seem larger than your capacity.

Commitment is what transforms them into realities.

Today, as the programme continues to grow year after year, I look back at those intense days with gratitude. Not because the work was difficult, but because it reminded me that some opportunities deserve everything you can give them.

The satisfaction, of course, is when they all love it. The satisfaction is that we could pull it off and the satisfaction is that it's entering its 4th year of this program, and today's is bigger than was imagined, by all of us.
